design_detail: Descriptive case series of four medico-legal autopsies of suspected drug overdose deaths. Blood was drawn separately (needle puncture after ligation or cross-clamping) from up to 11 vessel sites: pulmonary vein and artery, thoracic aorta, abdominal aorta and inferior vena cava above and below the renal veins, subclavian and femoral veins; also mixed cardiac blood (case 3) and portal venous blood (case 2), with cerebrospinal fluid, vitreous humour, bile, urine, solid organs and gastrointestinal contents. Drugs: doxepin (case 1); amobarbital, secobarbital and pentobarbital (case 2); clomipramine and flurazepam taken with chloral hydrate (case 3); imipramine, with lidocaine given in hospital (case 4). The only measurement in life is one hospital blood sample in case 4. Concentrations are reported descriptively; no statistics.
can_establish: That in four selected overdose deaths, concentrations of tricyclic antidepressants, barbiturates and flurazepam differed several-fold between blood samples taken from different vessels of the same body, usually highest in central vessels and lowest in subclavian or femoral veins (not in case 1), and that in the one case with a sample from life, every post-mortem blood sample, femoral included, was higher than that sample.
cannot_establish: How often or by how much such differences occur in deaths generally (four cases chosen to illustrate, no denominator); whether the differences arose after death rather than before it (no body was sampled at intervals after death; diffusion out of organs is the authors' inference); whether they apply to other drugs, including illicit drugs, or to deaths after ordinary amounts; or that any death after therapeutic doses has been misread as an overdose (no such case is studied).

sample.recruitment: Medico-legal autopsies: suspected drug overdoses identified before autopsy so that an extended protocol (many tissues and fluids, multiple blood samples) could be followed (p. 254, Materials and Methods). The office, period and number of eligible or sampled cases are not stated; the authors were at the University of Dundee and the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner, Edmonton, Alberta (p. 253).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not stated beyond suspected drug overdose identified before autopsy (p. 254).
sample.demographics: Case 1: man aged 23, 175 cm, 70 kg. Case 2: man aged 38, 180 cm, 87 kg, found dead in a remand-centre cell and described as known to inject oral pharmaceutical preparations. Case 3: woman aged 24, 165 cm, 64 kg. Case 4: man aged 47, 177 cm, 92 kg (pp. 254–259). No significant pre-existing natural disease at autopsy in any case.
sample.selection_effects: The cases were presented to illustrate the dramatic extent of the phenomenon (Abstract and Introduction, p. 253), so they are likely to be among the most striking; how many deaths were sampled with this protocol, and why these four were published, is not reported. All four were deaths after large ingestions (cases 1, 3 and 4 described as suicidal overdoses), three with unabsorbed drug still in the stomach or bowel (cases 1–3). The drugs are tricyclic antidepressants, barbiturates and flurazepam; the findings may not carry over to other drugs, including illicit drugs, or to deaths after ordinary amounts.

exposure.measurement: Post-mortem concentrations by gas chromatography with nitrogen–phosphorus detection (doxepin, imipramine, clomipramine and their desmethyl metabolites), high-performance liquid chromatography with UV detection at 214 nm (the three barbiturates) and gas chromatography with electron-capture detection (flurazepam, desalkylflurazepam); internal standards, a 5-point calibration before each set of samples, all specimens run in duplicate, independent in-house quality controls with each run (p. 254). No limits of detection, precision or recovery are given. Lidocaine (case 4) and trichloroethanol (case 3) results are reported without a described method, and the screening used to establish which drugs were present is not described.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Amounts taken are unknown. Described as suicidal overdoses of doxepin (case 1), of chloral hydrate, clomipramine and flurazepam (case 3) and of imipramine (case 4); in case 2 the stomach held a ruptured condom with granular debris, and no cause or manner of death is stated (pp. 254–259). Unabsorbed drug: tablet debris and two intact capsules in the duodenum (case 1, p. 254); 746, 993 and 903 mg of amobarbital, secobarbital and pentobarbital in the stomach contents (case 2, Table 2, p. 257); 2,400 mg of clomipramine and 9 mg of flurazepam in the stomach contents (case 3, Table 3, p. 258). Case 4 had gastric lavage with charcoal in hospital (p. 259).
exposure.polysubstance: Case 2: three barbiturates together. Case 3: chloral hydrate (its metabolite trichloroethanol measured only in mixed cardiac blood, 247 mg/l, and liver, 342 mg/kg), clomipramine and flurazepam. Case 4: lidocaine given intravenously in hospital (pp. 257–259). Case 1 is reported as doxepin and its metabolite only (p. 254). Ethanol is not reported for any case.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (deaths). Interval from death to autopsy sampling: case 1, 17 h after the body was found and 40 h after he was last known alive; case 2, 30 h after discovery and an estimated 36 h after death; case 3, an estimated 24–48 h after death; case 4, 7.25 h after death and 9.25 h after the hospital sample (pp. 254–259). Body position and storage before autopsy are not reported.

comparison.controls: No comparison group and no deaths from other causes. Comparisons are within each body (blood from different vessels, tissues and fluids) and, in case 4 only, with one hospital blood sample drawn on admission, about 1 h before cardiac arrest (p. 259).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Concentrations at the moment of death are unknown in all four cases. In case 4 the stated intervals place the hospital sample about 2 h before death, so absorption from the gut may have continued after it was drawn. No body was sampled more than once after death.

outcomes.instruments: Drug and metabolite concentrations in mg/l (blood and fluids), mg/kg (tissues) and mg (gastrointestinal contents) (Tables 1–4, pp. 256–260); blood concentrations by vessel plotted in Figures 1–4 (pp. 255–259); Figure 5 sets case 4 organ concentrations beside blood from nearby vessels (p. 260).
outcomes.validity_norms: No assay validation data are reported; there are no reference values for site differences.
outcomes.operationalization: Site dependence is shown as the spread of concentrations across blood samples from one body. That the spread is an artefact arising after death is the authors' inference from its size and pattern (pp. 260–262), not a change measured over time.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (descriptive values; no statistical tests).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported. Not material to instrumental assays, but the four cases were chosen for publication with their results known.

analysis.effect_sizes: Printed ranges (pp. 255–259): case 1, doxepin 3.6–12.5 and desmethyldoxepin 1.2–7.5 mg/l; case 2, amobarbital 4.3–25.8, secobarbital 3.9–25.3 and pentobarbital 5.1–31.5 mg/l in systemic blood, with portal venous blood at 40.9, 42.8 and 48.3 mg/l; case 3, clomipramine 4.0–21.5 and desmethylclomipramine 1.7–8.1 mg/l, mixed cardiac blood 15.3 and 4.1 mg/l, flurazepam 0.15–0.99 mg/l with mixed cardiac blood 0.51 mg/l; case 4, imipramine 4.1–18.1 and desipramine 1.0–3.6 mg/l against 2.3 and 0.6 mg/l in the hospital sample, lidocaine 0.9–1.4 mg/l. Editors' calculation, highest to lowest blood value within one body: doxepin 3.5-fold; amobarbital 6.0-, secobarbital 6.5- and pentobarbital 6.2-fold; clomipramine 5.4-fold; flurazepam 6.6-fold; imipramine 4.4-fold; lidocaine 1.6-fold. Case 4 post-mortem imipramine was 1.8 to 7.9 times the hospital value (4.1/2.3 and 18.1/2.3); the femoral veins, read from Figure 4 at 300 dpi, were about 5.0 and 5.6 mg/l, about 2.2–2.4 times it. In case 1 the femoral vein, read from Figure 1, was about 5.0 mg/l, about 0.4 times the pulmonary venous value and above the pulmonary artery (3.6) and thoracic aorta (4.4).
analysis.selective_reporting: Desalkylflurazepam was assayed (p. 254) but no result is reported; flurazepam blood values are given only as a range with the highest and lowest sites (p. 257). Whether other deaths were sampled with this protocol and not reported is unknown.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In four selected overdose deaths, blood concentrations of tricyclic antidepressants, barbiturates and flurazepam differed about 3.5- to 6.6-fold between vessels of the same body (editors' calculation), usually highest in the pulmonary vessels or in the inferior vena cava and lowest in subclavian or femoral veins; in case 1 the lowest doxepin value was in the pulmonary artery. In case 4 every post-mortem blood sample exceeded a hospital sample taken about an hour before cardiac arrest. Lidocaine, given in hospital and hardly concentrated in organs other than muscle and cerebral cortex, varied only 1.6-fold across the same samples (editors' calculation).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Abstract says the data suggest diffusion of drug out of solid organs into blood and states that the lowest levels were found in peripheral vessels (p. 253); the Discussion calls diffusion from solid organs the major factor while conceding that the cause is unresolved and probably multifactorial (pp. 261–262). The mechanism is inferred, not observed: no body was sampled at intervals after death, and the alternative the authors set aside with literature on arterial–venous differences, uneven distribution in life after a large ingestion that was still being absorbed, applied to all four cases and was not tested. The warning that an artefactually raised level after therapeutic doses may be misread as a lethal overdose (p. 262) cites a conference paper (ref. 14), not these overdose cases. The Abstract's peripheral-lowest generalization does not hold for case 1.

timeline.event: Jones & Pounder, a single detailed case study of site dependence of drug concentrations in post-mortem blood (ref. 9 of this paper; not read by this reader).

Leikin & Watson's review tabulates approximate heart-to-peripheral blood ratios for about 100 drugs (doxepin 5.5, imipramine 1.8 to 2.2, clomipramine 1.9), without case numbers or per-drug sources; it cites Pounder's 1993 book chapter, not this paper.

Ketola & Kriikku compile paired within-case ratios from the literature, with this paper among the doxepin sources: median ratio of other blood (such as cardiac blood) to femoral blood 1.27 across drugs, doxepin 1.61 (26 results).
Borra et al., a review of 50 years of post-mortem redistribution research (on the reading list; not read by this reader).

replication.where_it_stands: Site dependence of post-mortem blood concentrations has since been compiled across many drugs (Leikin & Watson 2003; Ketola & Kriikku 2019, both read in this batch), with central-to-femoral ratios usually smaller than the several-fold differences shown in these selected cases and varying widely between drugs and between cases. Neither later source settles how much of the difference arises after death rather than from incomplete distribution before death.

funding.funder: No funding statement. The Acknowledgements thank three named technical staff for the large number of drug determinations (p. 262).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article (1990).
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Forensic Medicine, University of Dundee, and Office of the Chief Medical Examiner, Edmonton, Alberta (p. 253). Two sources cited for key points are the authors' own: the 1987 case study (ref. 9) and Jones's 1988 conference paper on site-dependent differences (ref. 14). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: Repeated sampling of the same vessels from shortly after death until autopsy, in consecutive rather than selected deaths with known drug intake and, where possible, a blood level taken at or just before death, including deaths after ordinary therapeutic or recreational amounts, with body position and storage temperature recorded. This would separate change after death from uneven distribution before death and show how often a level is raised enough to change the conclusion about cause of death.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: Four autopsies of suspected overdoses chosen to illustrate the phenomenon; no frame (office, period, eligible deaths) is stated.
Selection to illustrate; how many deaths were sampled with the protocol and why these four were reported is not stated.
Four cases: enough to show that several-fold differences occur, not how often or how large they usually are.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Age, sex, body size, autopsy findings and intervals from death to autopsy are given; the office, period, body storage and position, and who decided cause and manner of death are not; case 2 has no stated cause or manner.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: All four cases are reported, but not every measured result (desalkylflurazepam; flurazepam by site), and whether other sampled deaths were left out is unknown.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Site-specific blood from ligated or cross-clamped vessels and chromatographic assays with internal standards, calibration, duplicates and quality controls; no validation data, and the condition of interest (change after death) is inferred from the pattern, not measured over time.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Same sampling technique throughout, but the set of sites differs between cases (one or both subclavian and femoral veins; mixed cardiac blood only in case 3; portal vein only in case 2) and death-to-sampling intervals range from 7.25 h to an estimated 48 h.
Descriptive concentrations only; no estimate to which statistics would apply.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The JBI items are applied to a small case series without a comparison group, as the round brief directs (the project's JBI instrument is the prevalence checklist; items 8 and 9 do not apply). The measurements appear careful (separately ligated vessels, duplicate assays with quality controls), so the concentrations are credible as measured; the risk lies in selection (four illustrative cases, no denominator) and in the inference about cause (no serial sampling), which together make the editors' summary high. Citable for: several-fold differences in tricyclic antidepressant, barbiturate and flurazepam concentrations between blood drawn from different vessels of the same body, usually central higher than femoral; and, in one case, every post-mortem sample including femoral blood above a sample taken in hospital before death. Not citable for: how often or by how much this happens in deaths generally, the mechanism, illicit drugs, or deaths after therapeutic doses being misclassified as overdoses (not studied here).

key_findings.finding: Case 1 (suicidal doxepin overdose; autopsy 17 h after the body was found and 40 h after he was last known alive): blood doxepin 3.6–12.5 mg/l and desmethyldoxepin 1.2–7.5 mg/l across nine vessel sites; highest in the pulmonary vein, the other sites varying over a small range; pulmonary artery 3.6 and 1.8 mg/l, thoracic aorta 4.4 and 1.6 mg/l.
key_findings.locator: Results › Case 1 (5208), 1st and 2nd paragraphs (the 2nd continuing on p. 255); Fig. 1 (p. 255)
key_findings.note: Read from Figure 1 at 300 dpi (approximate): femoral vein doxepin about 5.0 mg/l and subclavian about 5.1 mg/l, both above the pulmonary artery (3.6) and thoracic aorta (4.4). The lowest desmethyldoxepin bar is about 1.5 mg/l, not the printed 1.2 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Case 2 (man found dead in a remand-centre cell, ruptured condom and granular debris in the stomach; autopsy 30 h after discovery and an estimated 36 h after death): systemic blood amobarbital 4.3–25.8, secobarbital 3.9–25.3 and pentobarbital 5.1–31.5 mg/l, highest in the inferior vena cava above the renal veins and lowest in the right femoral vein; portal venous blood 40.9, 42.8 and 48.3 mg/l; of the solid organs only the liver concentrated the drugs (61, 74 and 89 mg/kg).
key_findings.locator: Results › Case 2 (5202), 2nd paragraph (p. 255, continuing on p. 256); Fig. 2 (p. 256); Table 2 (p. 257)
key_findings.note: The lowest site (right femoral vein) is read from Figure 2, whose bars there match the printed minima (about 4.4, 4.0 and 5.1 mg/l at 300 dpi).

key_findings.finding: Case 3 (suicidal overdose of chloral hydrate, clomipramine and flurazepam; autopsy an estimated 24–48 h after death): clomipramine 4.0–21.5 and desmethylclomipramine 1.7–8.1 mg/l across vessels, highest in the pulmonary artery and vein and lowest in the femoral veins; mixed cardiac blood 15.3 and 4.1 mg/l. Flurazepam 0.15–0.99 mg/l, highest in the inferior vena cava below the renal veins and lowest in the subclavian and femoral veins; mixed cardiac blood 0.51 mg/l.
key_findings.locator: Results › Case 3 (5269), 2nd paragraph (p. 257, continuing on p. 259); Fig. 3 (p. 258)

key_findings.finding: Case 4 (suicidal imipramine overdose treated in hospital with gastric lavage, charcoal and intravenous lidocaine; autopsy 7.25 h after death): a blood sample drawn on admission, about 1 h before cardiac arrest, held imipramine 2.3 and desipramine 0.6 mg/l and no lidocaine; post-mortem blood held imipramine 4.1–18.1 and desipramine 1.0–3.6 mg/l, lowest in the subclavian and femoral veins, high in the aorta and the inferior vena cava above the renal veins, highest in the pulmonary vein. Lidocaine ranged 0.9–1.4 mg/l in the same samples. Editors' calculation: every post-mortem sample exceeded the hospital value, by 1.8- to 7.9-fold.
key_findings.note: Read from Figure 4 at 300 dpi (approximate): left and right femoral veins about 5.0 and 5.6 mg/l imipramine, about 2.2–2.4 times the hospital value. The stated intervals place the hospital sample about 2 h before death (autopsy 9.25 h after the sample and 7.25 h after death).

key_findings.finding: Editors' calculation from the printed ranges, highest to lowest blood concentration within one body: doxepin 3.5-fold (case 1); amobarbital 6.0-, secobarbital 6.5- and pentobarbital 6.2-fold (case 2); clomipramine 5.4- and flurazepam 6.6-fold (case 3); imipramine 4.4-fold and lidocaine 1.6-fold (case 4).

Tricyclic antidepressants were concentrated in liver and lung: case 1 doxepin 62 mg/kg in liver, 73 and 26 mg/kg in the left and right lungs and 70 mg/kg in renal cortex, against 7.5–10.8 mg/kg in skeletal muscle; case 4 imipramine 136 mg/kg in liver and 100 mg/kg in lungs, against 16–24 mg/kg in skeletal muscle. In case 4, the relative concentrations in organs broadly paralleled those in blood from each organ's associated vessels.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (p. 256); Results › Case 4, 2nd paragraph (p. 259); Table 4 and Fig. 5 (p. 260)

key_findings.finding: Unabsorbed drug remained in the gut in cases 1–3: tablet debris and two intact capsules in the duodenum (case 1); 746, 993 and 903 mg of amobarbital, secobarbital and pentobarbital in the stomach contents with further amounts along the small bowel (case 2); 2,400 mg of clomipramine and 9 mg of flurazepam in the stomach contents (case 3).

The authors argue that arterial–venous differences in life and the variable make-up of post-mortem blood cannot explain differences this large (in their earlier case they found no correlation between drug concentration and haemoglobin content), and propose diffusion after death along concentration gradients from organs holding high concentrations, especially liver and lung, into nearby vessels; they state that the cause remains unresolved and is probably multifactorial.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 260, continuing on p. 261), 2nd, 3rd and 5th paragraphs (p. 261)

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that a post-mortem blood concentration may differ several-fold from the true concentration at death; that after therapeutic doses an artefactually raised level could be misread as a lethal overdose (citing ref. 14); that predicting the dose taken from post-mortem blood is invalid for some drugs (citing ref. 5); and that databases of post-mortem blood concentrations lose reference value when the sampling site is unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: The Abstract states that the lowest levels were found in peripheral vessels such as the subclavian and femoral veins, but in case 1 the lowest doxepin concentration (3.6 mg/l) was in the pulmonary artery and the femoral vein (about 5.0 mg/l, read from Figure 1) exceeded several central sites; the Results themselves say the case 1 samples other than the pulmonary vein varied over a small range.
reporting_issues.consequence: The central-high, peripheral-low pattern held in three of four cases; it should not be cited as universal even within this series.

reporting_issues.issue: The Abstract and Results give 1.2 mg/l as the lowest desmethyldoxepin blood concentration in case 1, but no bar in Figure 1 lies below about 1.5 mg/l (enlarged crop of the figure; the pulmonary artery bar at 1.8 matches the text).
reporting_issues.consequence: Either a sample is missing from the figure or a value is misprinted; the metabolite's spread would be about 5-fold rather than 6.3-fold if the minimum is 1.5 (editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: Materials and Methods describe an assay for desalkylflurazepam, but no result for it is reported; lidocaine (case 4) and trichloroethanol (case 3) results are reported without any described method.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the lidocaine values, which show little site variation, rest on an undescribed assay.

reporting_issues.issue: Case 4's hospital sample is described as drawn about 1 h before cardiac arrest, while the stated intervals (autopsy 9.25 h after the sample and 7.25 h after death) place it about 2 h before death; the course in between and its bearing on the comparison are not discussed.
reporting_issues.consequence: Absorption from the gut may have continued after the sample was drawn, so the excess of post-mortem over hospital values cannot be attributed wholly to change after death.

reporting_issues.issue: The office, period and number of deaths sampled with the protocol are not reported, the four cases were chosen to illustrate the phenomenon, and case 2's cause and manner of death are not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: The series shows that large site differences occur, not how often; how the deaths were classified cannot be checked.
